Constructive DD-module Theory with Singular

Daniel Andres    Michael Brickenstein    Viktor Levandovskyy    Jorge Martín-Morales    Hans Schönemann
Abstract

We overview numerous algorithms in computational DD-module theory together with the theoretical background as well as the implementation in the computer algebra system Singular. We discuss new approaches to the computation of Bernstein operators, of logarithmic annihilator of a polynomial, of annihilators of rational functions as well as complex powers of polynomials. We analyze algorithms for local Bernstein-Sato polynomials and also algorithms, recovering any kind of Bernstein-Sato polynomial from partial knowledge of its roots. We address a novel way to compute the Bernstein-Sato polynomial for an affine variety algorithmically. All the carefully selected nontrivial examples, which we present, have been computed with our implementation. We address such applications as the computation of a zeta-function for certain integrals and revealing the algebraic dependence between pairwise commuting elements.

Mathematics Subject Classification (2010). 13P10, 14F10, 68W30.

Keywords. DD-modules, non-commutative Gröbner bases, annihilator ideal, bb-function, Bernstein-Sato polynomial, Bernstein-Sato ideal.

1 Introduction

Constructive DD-module theory has been dynamically developing throughout the last years. There are new approaches, algorithms, implementations and applications. Our work on the implementation of procedures for DD-modules started in 2003, motivated among other factors by challenging elimination problems in non-commutative algebras, which appear e. g. in algorithms for computing Bernstein-Sato polynomials. We reported on solving several challenges in [20]. A non-commutative subsystem Singular:Plural [14] of the computer algebra system Singular provides a user with possibilities to compute numerous Gröbner bases-based procedures in a wide class of non-commutative GG-algebras [22]. It was natural to use this functionality in the context of computational DD-module theory. Nowadays we present a DD-module suite in Singular consisting of the libraries dmod.lib, dmodapp.lib, dmodvar.lib and bfun.lib. There are many useful and flexible procedures for various aspects of DD-module theory. These libraries are freely distributed together with Singular [11].

There are several implementations of algorithms for DD-modules, namely the experimental program kan/sm1 by N. Takayama [38], the bfct package in Risa/Asir [31] by M. Noro [30] and the package Dmodules.m2 in Macaulay2 by A. Leykin and H. Tsai [40]. We aim at creating a DD-module suite, which will combine flexibility and rich functionality with high performance, being able to treat more complicated examples.

In this paper we do not present any comparison between different computer algebra systems in the realm of DD-modules, referring to [20] and [1]. However, comparison in the latter articles shows, that our implementation is superior to kan/sm1 and Macaulay2 and in many cases more powerful than Risa/Asir.

Here is the list of problems we address in this paper:

  • •

    ss-parametric annihilator of ff (Section 3, see also [20, 1]),

  • •

    annihilator of fαf^{\alpha} for α∈ℂ\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}} (Section 4, see also [34]),

  • •

    annihilator of a polynomial function ff and of a rational function f/gf/g (Section 4),

  • •

    bb-function with respect to weights for an ideal (Section 5, see also [1]),

  • •

    global and local Bernstein-Sato polynomials of ff (Section 6),

  • •

    partial knowledge of Bernstein-Sato polynomial (Section 6.4, see also [20]),

  • •

    Bernstein operator of ff (Section 7),

  • •

    logarithmic annihilator of ff (Section 8),

  • •

    Bernstein-Sato ideals for f=f1⋅…⋅fmf=f_{1}\cdot\ldots\cdot f_{m} (Section 9, see also [20]),

  • •

    annihilator and Bernstein-Sato polynomial for a variety (Section 10, see also [1]).

We describe both theoretical and implementational aspects of the problems above and illustrate them with carefully selected nontrivial examples, computed with our implementation in Singular. In Section 3.3, we give yet another alternative proof for the algorithm by Briançon-Maisonobe for computing AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)\ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s}), presented in [1]. Notably, this delivers additional structural information. In Section 7, we compare several approaches for the computation of Bernstein operators. Using the method of principal intersection, we formalize several methods for computing Bernstein-Sato polynomials. Following Budur et al. [7] and [1], we report on the implementation of two methods for the computation of Bernstein-Sato polynomials for affine varieties in a framework, which is a natural generalization of our approach to the algorithm by Briançon-Maisonobe.

Notations. Throughout the article 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is assumed to be a field of characteristic zero. By RR we denote the polynomial ring 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] and by f∈Rf\in R a non-constant polynomial.

We consider the nn-th Weyl algebra as the algebra of linear partial differential operators with polynomials coefficients. That is Dn=D(R)=𝕂⟨x1,…,xn,∂1,…,∂n∣{∂ixi=xi∂i+1,∂ixj=xj∂i,i≠j}⟩D_{n}=D(R)={\mathbb{K}}\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{n},\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{n}\mid\{\partial_{i}x_{i}=x_{i}\partial_{i}+1,\partial_{i}x_{j}=x_{j}\partial_{i},i\not=j\}\rangle. We denote by Dn​[s]=D⁡(R)⊗𝕂𝕂⁡[s1,…,sn]D_{n}[s]=D(R)\otimes_{{\mathbb{K}}}{\mathbb{K}}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}] and drop the index nn depending on the context.

The ring RR is a natural Dn​(R)D_{n}(R)-module with the action

xi∙f(x1,…,xn)=xi⋅f(x1,…,xn),∂i∙f(x1,…,xn)=∂f⁡(x1,…,xn)∂xi.x_{i}\bullet f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=x_{i}\cdot f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}),\quad\partial_{i}\bullet f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\frac{\partial f(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})}{\partial x_{i}}.

Working with monomial orderings in elimination, we use the notation x≫yx\gg y for “xx is greater than any power of yy”.

Given an associative 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebra AA and some monomial well-ordering on AA, we denote by lm⁡(f)\lm(f) (resp. lc⁡(f)\lc(f)) the leading monomial (resp. the leading coefficient) of f∈Af\in A. Given a left Gröbner basis G⊂AG\subset A and f∈Af\in A, we denote by NF⁡(f,G)\NF(f,G) the normal form of ff with respect to the left ideal ⟨G⟩A{}_{A}\langle G\rangle. We also use the shorthand notation h→Hfh\rightarrow_{H}f (and h→fh\rightarrow f, if HH is clear from the context) for the reduction of h∈Ah\in A to f∈Af\in A with respect to the set HH. If not specified, under ideal we mean left ideal. For a,b∈Aa,b\in A, we use the Lie bracket notation [a,b]:=a​b−b​a[a,b]:=ab-ba as well as the skew Lie bracket notation [a,b]k:=a​b−k⋅b​a[a,b]_{k}:=ab-k\cdot ba for k∈𝕂∗k\in{\mathbb{K}}^{*}.

It is convenient to treat the algebras we deal with in a bigger framework of GG-algebras of Lie type.

Definition 1.1.

Let AA be the quotient of the free associative algebra 𝕂⁡⟨x1,…,xn⟩{\mathbb{K}}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\rangle by the two-sided ideal II, generated by the finite set {xj​xi−xi​xj−di​j}​∀1≤i<j≤n\{x_{j}x_{i}-x_{i}x_{j}-d_{ij}\}\;\forall 1\leq i<j\leq n, where di​j∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]d_{ij}\in{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. AA is called a GG–algebra of Lie type [22], if
∙\bullet   ∀ 1≤i<j<k≤n\forall\;1\leq i<j<k\leq n the expression di​j​xk−xk​di​j+xj​di​k−di​k​xj+dj​k​xi−xi​dj​kd_{ij}x_{k}-x_{k}d_{ij}+x_{j}d_{ik}-d_{ik}x_{j}+d_{jk}x_{i}-x_{i}d_{jk} reduces to zero modulo II and,
∙\bullet there exists a monomial ordering ≺\prec on 𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], such that lm⁡(di​j)≺xi​xj\lm(d_{ij})\prec x_{i}x_{j}, ∀i<j\forall i<j.

GG-algebras are also known as algebras of solvable type [17, 23] and PBW algebras [8]. We often use the following.

Lemma 1.2 (Generalized Product Criterion, [22]).

Let AA be a GG-algebra of Lie type and f,g∈Af,g\in A. Suppose lm⁡(f)\lm(f) and lm⁡(g)\lm(g) have no common factors, then spoly(f,g)→{f,g}[f,g]\spoly(f,g)\rightarrow_{\{f,g\}}[f,g].

2 Challenges for Gröbner bases engines of Singular

Since the very beginning of implementation of algorithms for DD-modules in Singular there have been intensive interaction with the developers of Singular. Numerous challenging examples and open problems from constructive DD-module theory were approached both on the level of libraries and in the kernel of Singular and Singular:Plural. This resulted in several enhancements in kernel procedures and, among other, motivated M. Brickenstein to develop and implement the generalization of his slimgb [6] (slim Gröbner basis) algorithm to non-commutative GG-algebras. Indeed slimgb is a variant of Buchberger’s algorithm. It is designed to keep polynomials slim, that is short with small coefficients. The algorithm features parallel reductions and a strategy to minimize the weighted lengths of polynomials. A weighted length function of a polynomial can be seen as measure for the intermediate expression swell and it can consider not only the number of terms in a polynomial, but also their coefficients and degrees. Considering the degrees of the terms inside the polynomials, slimgb can often directly (that is, without using Gröbner Walk or similar algorithms) compute Gröbner bases with respect to e. g. elimination orderings. The procedure slimgb demonstrated very good performance on examples from the realm of DD-modules [20], which require computations with elimination orderings.

As it will be seen in the paper, various computational questions, arising in DD-module theory, use much more than Gröbner bases only. Among other, a transformation matrix between two bases (called Lift in [15]), the kernel of a module homomorphism (called Modulo in [15]) and so on must be applied for complicated examples. On the other hand, the standard std routine for Gröbner bases, generalized to non-commutative GG-algebras, is used together with slimgb for a variety of problems. Since the beginning of development of the DD-module suite in Singular, these functions have been enhanced: they became much faster and more flexible. The effect of the use of the generalized Chain Criterion (cf. [15]) in Gröbner engines is even bigger in the non-commutative case, due to the discarding of multiplications, which complexity is increased, compared with the commutative case. On the contrary, the generalized Product Criterion (Lemma 1.2) plays a minor role in the implementation, since the complete discarding of a pair generalizes to the computation of a Lie bracket of the pair members.

The concept of ring list, introduced in Singular in 2004, enormously simplified the process of creation and modification of rings (like changing the monomial module ordering, regrouping of variables, modifying non-commutative relations, working with parameters of the ground field etc.). Especially in the DD-module setting we modify rings often, create a new one from existing rings and equip a new ring with a new ordering. Thus, with ring lists the development of such procedures became much easier and the corresponding code became much more manageable.

We have to mention, that in the meantime the implementation of non-commutative multiplication in the kernel of Singular:Plural has been improved as well.

3 ss-parametric annihilator of ff

Recall Malgrange’s construction for f=f1⋯fp∈𝕂[x1,…,xn]f=f_{1}\cdots f_{p}\in{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Consider the algebra Wp+nW_{p+n}, being the (p+n)(p+n)-th Weyl algebra

𝕂⟨{tj,∂tj∣1≤j≤p}∣{[∂tj,tk]=δj​k}⟩⊗𝕂𝕂⟨{xi,∂i∣1≤i≤n}∣{[∂i,xk]=δi​k}⟩.{\mathbb{K}}\langle\{t_{j},{\partial t}_{j}\mid 1\leq j\leq p\}\mid\{[{\partial t}_{j},t_{k}]=\delta_{jk}\}\rangle\otimes_{{\mathbb{K}}}{\mathbb{K}}\langle\{x_{i},\partial_{i}\mid 1\leq i\leq n\}\mid\{[\partial_{i},x_{k}]=\delta_{ik}\}\rangle.

Moreover, consider the left ideal in Wp+nW_{p+n}, called Malgrange ideal

If:=⟨{tj−fj,∑j=1p∂fj∂xi∂tj+∂i∣1≤j≤p,1≤i≤n}⟩.I_{f}:=\langle\;\{\;t_{j}-f_{j},\sum^{p}_{j=1}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}{\partial t}_{j}+\partial_{i}\;\mid 1\leq j\leq p,1\leq i\leq n\}\;\rangle.

Then for s=(s1,…,sp)s=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{p}) we denote fs:=f1s1⋯fpspf^{s}:=f_{1}^{s_{1}}\cdots f_{p}^{s_{p}}. Let us compute

If∩𝕂[{tj∂tj}]⟨xi,∂xi∣[∂i,xi]=1⟩⊂Dn[{tj∂tj}]I_{f}\cap{\mathbb{K}}[\{t_{j}\partial t_{j}\}]\langle x_{i},\partial x_{i}\mid[\partial_{i},x_{i}]=1\rangle\subset D_{n}[\{t_{j}\partial t_{j}\}]

and furthermore, replace tj​∂tjt_{j}\partial t_{j} with −sj−1-s_{j}-1. The result is known (e. g. [34]) to coincide with the ss-parametric annihilator of fsf^{s}, AnnDn​[s](fs)={Q(x,∂,s)∈Dn[s]∣Q∙fs=0}\Ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s})=\{Q(x,\partial,s)\in D_{n}[s]\mid Q\bullet f^{s}=0\}.

There exist several methods for the computation of ss-parametric annihilator of fsf^{s}.

3.1 Oaku and Takayama

The algorithm by Oaku and Takayama [32, 34] was developed in a wider context and uses homogenization. Consider the 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}-algebras T:=𝕂⁡[t1,…,tp]T:={\mathbb{K}}[t_{1},\ldots,t_{p}], Dp′:=D⁡(T)D^{\prime}_{p}:=D(T) and H:=Dn⊗𝕂Dp′⊗𝕂𝕂[u1,…,up,v1,…,vp]H:=D_{n}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}D^{\prime}_{p}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}{\mathbb{K}}[u_{1},\ldots,u_{p},v_{1},\ldots,v_{p}]. Moreover, let II below be the (u,v)(u,v)-homogenized Malgrange ideal, that is the left ideal in HH

I=⟨{tj−ujfj,∑k=1p∂fk∂xiuk∂tj+∂i,ujvj−1}⟩.I=\left\langle\{t_{j}-u_{j}f_{j},\sum^{p}_{k=1}\frac{\partial f_{k}}{\partial x_{i}}u_{k}{\partial t}_{j}+\partial_{i},u_{j}v_{j}-1\}\right\rangle.

Oaku and Takayama proved, that AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)\ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s}) can be obtained in two steps. At first {uj,vj}\{u_{j},v_{j}\} are eliminated from II with the help of Gröbner bases, thus yielding I′=I∩(Dn⊗𝕂Dp′)I^{\prime}=I\cap(D_{n}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}D^{\prime}_{p}). Then, one calculates I′∩(Dn⊗𝕂𝕂[{−tj∂tj−1}])I^{\prime}\cap(D_{n}\otimes_{\mathbb{K}}{\mathbb{K}}[\{-t_{j}\partial t_{j}-1\}]) and substitutes every appearance of tj​∂tjt_{j}\partial t_{j} by −sj−1-s_{j}-1 in the latter. The result is then AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)\ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s}).

3.2 Briançon and Maisonobe

Consider Sp=𝕂⟨{∂tj,sj}∣∂tjsk=sk∂tj−δj​k∂tj⟩S_{p}={\mathbb{K}}\langle\{\partial t_{j},s_{j}\}\mid\partial t_{j}s_{k}=s_{k}\partial t_{j}-\delta_{jk}\partial t_{j}\rangle (the pp-th shift algebra) and S′=Dn⊗𝕂SpS^{\prime}=D_{n}\otimes_{{\mathbb{K}}}S_{p}. Moreover, consider the following left ideal in S′S^{\prime}:

I=⟨{sj+fj∂tj,∑k=1p∂fk∂xi∂tk+∂i}⟩.I=\left\langle\{s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j},\sum^{p}_{k=1}\frac{\partial f_{k}}{\partial x_{i}}{\partial t}_{k}+\partial_{i}\}\right\rangle.

Briançon and Maisonobe proved [5] that AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)=I∩Dn​[s1,…,sp]\ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s})=I\cap D_{n}[s_{1},\ldots,s_{p}] and hence the latter can be computed via the left Gröbner basis with respect to an elimination ordering for {∂tj}\{\partial t_{j}\}.

3.3 Another alternative proof of Briançon-Maisonobe’s method

Here we give yet another [1] computer algebraic proof for the method by Briançon and Maisonobe.

Throughout this section, we assume 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n and 1≤j≤p1\leq j\leq p. Define

E:=𝕂⟨{tj,∂tj,xi,∂i,sj}∣{[∂i,xi]=1,[∂tj,tj]=1,[tk,sj]=δj​ktj,[∂tk,sj]=−δj​k∂tj}⟩.E:={\mathbb{K}}\langle\{t_{j},\partial t_{j},x_{i},\partial_{i},s_{j}\}\mid\{[\partial_{i},x_{i}]=1,[\partial t_{j},t_{j}]=1,[t_{k},s_{j}]=\delta_{jk}t_{j},[\partial t_{k},s_{j}]=-\delta_{jk}\partial t_{j}\}\rangle.

Let B=Dn​[s]B=D_{n}[s] be a subalgebra of EE, generated by {xi,∂i,sj}\{x_{i},\partial_{i},s_{j}\}. Then the Briançon-Maisonobe method requires to prove [1], that

⟨{tj−fj,∑j=1p∂fj∂xi∂tj+∂i,fj∂tj+sj}⟩∩Dn[s]=AnnDn​[s](fs).\langle\{t_{j}-f_{j},\sum^{p}_{j=1}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}{\partial t}_{j}+\partial_{i},f_{j}\partial t_{j}+s_{j}\}\rangle\cap D_{n}[s]=\ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s}).
Theorem 3.1.

Let us define the following polynomials and sets:

gi:=∂i+∑k=1p∂fk∂xi∂tk,G={gi},T={tj−fj},S={sj+fj∂tj}.g_{i}:=\partial_{i}+\sum^{p}_{k=1}\frac{\partial f_{k}}{\partial x_{i}}{\partial t}_{k},\ G=\{g_{i}\},T=\{t_{j}-f_{j}\},S=\{s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j}\}.

Let Λ\Lambda be a (possibly empty) subset of {1,…,p}\{1,\ldots,p\}. Define MΛ:=G∪{tk−fk∣k∈Λ}∪{sj+fj​∂tj∣j∈{1,…,p}∖Λ}M_{\Lambda}:=G\cup\{t_{k}-f_{k}\mid k\in\Lambda\}\cup\{s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j}\mid j\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\setminus\Lambda\}.

  1. (a)

    For any Λ\Lambda, the elements of MΛM_{\Lambda} commute pairwise. In particular, so do G∪TG\cup T and G∪SG\cup S.

  2. (b)

    Consider an ordering ≺\prec, satisfying {tj}≫{xi}\{t_{j}\}\gg\{x_{i}\}, {∂i,sj}≫{xi,∂tj}\{\partial_{i},s_{j}\}\gg\{x_{i},\partial t_{j}\}. Then any subset of G∪T∪SG\cup T\cup S is a left Gröbner basis with respect to ≺\prec. In particular, so is the set MΛM_{\Lambda} for any Λ\Lambda.

  3. (c)

    The elements of MΛM_{\Lambda} are algebraically independent.

  4. (d)

    For any Λ\Lambda, the Krull (and hence the Gel’fand-Kirillov) dimension of 𝕂⁡[MΛ]{\mathbb{K}}[M_{\Lambda}] is n+pn+p.

  5. (e)

    For any Λ\Lambda, 𝕂⁡[MΛ]{\mathbb{K}}[M_{\Lambda}] is a maximal commutative subalgebra of EE.

Proof.

(a) Computing commutators between elements, we obtain

[gi,gk]=∂tj∑j[∂i,∂fj∂xk]+∂tj∑j[∂fj∂xi,∂k]=∂tj∑j([∂i,∂fj∂xk]−[∂k,∂fj∂xi])=0,\displaystyle[g_{i},g_{k}]={\partial t}_{j}\sum_{j}[\partial_{i},\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{k}}]+{\partial t}_{j}\sum_{j}[\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}},\partial_{k}]={\partial t}_{j}\sum_{j}([\partial_{i},\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{k}}]-[\partial_{k},\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}])=0,
[tk−fk,gi]=∑j∂fj∂xi[tk,∂tj]−[fk,∂i]=0,[ti−fi,tk−fk]=0,\displaystyle[t_{k}-f_{k},g_{i}]=\sum_{j}\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}[t_{k},\partial t_{j}]-[f_{k},\partial_{i}]=0,\qquad[t_{i}-f_{i},t_{k}-f_{k}]=0,
[si+fi∂ti,sj+fj∂tj]=fj[si,∂tj]−fi[sj,∂ti]=0,[sj+fj∂tj,gi]=[sj,∂i]+\displaystyle[s_{i}+f_{i}\partial t_{i},s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j}]=f_{j}[s_{i},\partial t_{j}]-f_{i}[s_{j},\partial t_{i}]=0,\qquad[s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j},g_{i}]=[s_{j},\partial_{i}]+
+∂tj[fj,∂i]+∑k=1p∂fk∂xi[sj,∂tk]+[fj∂tj,∑k=1p∂fk∂xi∂tk]=∂fj∂xi∂tj−[∂i,fj]∂tj=0.\displaystyle+\partial t_{j}[f_{j},\partial_{i}]+\sum^{p}_{k=1}\frac{\partial f_{k}}{\partial x_{i}}[s_{j},{\partial t}_{k}]+[f_{j}\partial t_{j},\sum^{p}_{k=1}\frac{\partial f_{k}}{\partial x_{i}}{\partial t}_{k}]=\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial x_{i}}{\partial t}_{j}-[\partial_{i},f_{j}]\partial t_{j}=0.
The only nonzero commutator arises from
[tk−fk,sj+fj​∂tj]=[tk,sj]+fj​[tk,∂tj]−[fk,sj]−[fk,fj​∂tj]=δj​k​(tk−fk).\displaystyle[t_{k}-f_{k},s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j}]=[t_{k},s_{j}]+f_{j}[t_{k},\partial t_{j}]-[f_{k},s_{j}]-[f_{k},f_{j}\partial t_{j}]=\delta_{jk}(t_{k}-f_{k}).

However, according to the definition, only one of these elements belongs to MΛM_{\Lambda} for any Λ\Lambda.

(b) We run Buchberger’s algorithm by hands. Due to the ordering property, for each pair the generalized Product Criterion is applicable. Hence using (a) we see, that most ss-polynomials reduce to commutators, which are zero except spoly⁡(tk−fk,sj+fj​∂tj)=δj​k​(tk−fk)\spoly(t_{k}-f_{k},s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j})=\delta_{jk}(t_{k}-f_{k}), which reduces to zero modulo the first polynomial. Thus, any subset including MΛM_{\Lambda} is indeed a Gröbner basis.

(c) Using pairwise commutativity, we employ the Commutative Preimage Theorem from [19]. It states, that the ideal of algebraic dependencies between pairwise commuting elements {hk∣1≤k≤m}⊂E\{h_{k}\mid 1\leq k\leq m\}\subset E can be computed as

E⊗𝕂𝕂⁡[c1,…,cm]⊃⟨{hi−ci}⟩∩𝕂⁡[c1,…,cm],E\otimes_{{\mathbb{K}}}{\mathbb{K}}[c_{1},\ldots,c_{m}]\supset\langle\{h_{i}-c_{i}\}\rangle\cap{\mathbb{K}}[c_{1},\ldots,c_{m}],

where cic_{i} are new commutative variables, adjoint to EE. In this elimination problem one requires an ordering on E⊗𝕂𝕂⁡[c]E\otimes_{{\mathbb{K}}}{\mathbb{K}}[c], preferring variables of EE to cic_{i}’s. For such an ordering, one needs to compute a Gröbner basis. Now, take {hi}:=MΛ\{h_{i}\}:=M_{\Lambda}, 1≤i≤p+n1\leq i\leq p+n, and run Buchberger’s algorithm with respect to the same ordering as in (b). Thus we are again in the situation, where the Product Criterion applies, hence [hi−ci,hk−ck]=0[h_{i}-c_{i},h_{k}-c_{k}]=0 since [hi,hk]=0[h_{i},h_{k}]=0 by (b) and cic_{i} are central. Hence, {hi−ci}\{h_{i}-c_{i}\} is a left Gröbner basis and by the elimination property ⟨{hi−ci}⟩∩𝕂⁡[c1,…,cm]=0\langle\{h_{i}-c_{i}\}\rangle\cap{\mathbb{K}}[c_{1},\ldots,c_{m}]=0, that is {hi}\{h_{i}\} are algebraically independent.

(d) By (c), MΛM_{\Lambda} generates a commutative ring with no algebraic dependence between its elements, so the Krull dimension is the cardinality of MΛM_{\Lambda}, that is n+pn+p. Since MΛM_{\Lambda} is isomorphic to a commutative polynomial ring by (c), its Gel’fand-Kirillov dimension over the field 𝕂{\mathbb{K}} is n+pn+p as well.

(e) With respect to the ordering from (b), the leading monomials of the generators are {∂1,…,∂n}∪{tk∣k∈Λ}∪{sj∣j∉Λ}\{\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\}\cup\{t_{k}\mid k\in\Lambda\}\cup\{s_{j}\mid j\not\in\Lambda\}. Assume, that there exists an element in E∖𝕂⁡[MΛ]E\setminus{\mathbb{K}}[M_{\Lambda}], which commutes with all elements in MΛM_{\Lambda}. Then its leading monomial must belong to the subalgebra FF, generated by {x1,…,xn}∪{sk∣k∈Λ}∪{tj∣j∉Λ}∪{∂t1,…,∂tp}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\cup\{s_{k}\mid k\in\Lambda\}\cup\{t_{j}\mid j\not\in\Lambda\}\cup\{\partial t_{1},\ldots,\partial t_{p}\}. Since the center of EE is 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}, we consider centralizers of elements. Taking F′=∩k∈ΛC(tk−fk)∩FF^{\prime}=\cap_{k\in\Lambda}C(t_{k}-f_{k})\cap F, we see that an element from it can have no {∂tk,sk∣k∈Λ}\{\partial t_{k},s_{k}\mid k\in\Lambda\}. Considering F′′=∩iC(gi)∩F′F^{\prime\prime}=\cap_{i}C(g_{i})\cap F^{\prime}, we exclude {x1,…,xn}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}. Thus we are left with the subalgebra, generated by F~={∂tj,sj∣j∉Λ}\tilde{F}=\{\partial t_{j},s_{j}\mid j\not\in\Lambda\}. But no element of it can commute with {sj+fj​∂tj∣j∉Λ}\{s_{j}+f_{j}\partial t_{j}\mid j\not\in\Lambda\} except constants. Hence the claim. ∎

We want to eliminate both {tj}\{t_{j}\} and {∂tj}\{\partial t_{j}\} from an ideal, generated by G∪S∪TG\cup S\cup T. By using an elimination ordering for {tj}\{t_{j}\} we proved in (b) above, that G∪S∪TG\cup S\cup T is a Gröbner basis. Hence, the elimination ideal is generated by G∪SG\cup S and we can proceed with eliminating {∂tj}\{\partial t_{j}\} from G∪SG\cup S, which is exactly the statement of Briançon-Maisonobe in Section 3.2.

3.4 Implementation

We use the following acronyms in addressing functions in the implementation: OT for Oaku and Takayama, LOT for Levandovskyy’s modification of Oaku and Takayama [20] and BM for Briançon-Maisonobe. Moreover, it is possible to specify the desired Gröbner basis engine (std or slimgb) via an optional argument.

For the classical situation f=f1f=f_{1}, the procedure Sannfs(ff) computing AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)⊂Dn​[s]\Ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s})\subset D_{n}[s] uses a “minimal user knowledge” principle and chooses one of three mentioned algorithms. Alternatively, one can call the corresponding procedures SannfsOT, SannfsLOT, SannfsBM directly.

For the annihilator of f=f1⋯fpf=f_{1}\cdots f_{p}, see Section 9.

Example 3.2.

We demonstrate, how to compute the ss-parametric annihilator with Sannfs. This procedure takes a polynomial in a commutative ring as its argument and returns back a Weyl algebra of the type ring containing an object of the type ideal called LD. Note, that the latter ideal is a set of generators and not a Gröbner basis in general.

LIB "dmod.lib";
ring r = 0,(x,y),dp;          // set up the commutative ring
poly f = x^3 + y^2 + x*y^2;   // define the polynomial
def D = Sannfs(f); setring D; // call Sannfs and change to ring D
LD = groebner(LD); LD;        // compute and print Groebner basis
==> LD[1]=2*x*y*Dx-3*x^2*Dy-y^2*Dy+2*y*Dx
==> LD[2]=2*x^2*Dx+2*x*y*Dy+2*x*Dx+3*y*Dy-6*x*s-6*s
==> LD[3]=x^2*y*Dy+y^3*Dy-2*x^2*Dx-3*x*y*Dy-2*y^2*s+6*x*s
==> LD[4]=x^3*Dy+x*y^2*Dy+y^2*Dy-2*x*y*s-2*y*s
==> LD[5]=2*y^3*Dx*Dy+3*x^3*Dy^2+x*y^2*Dy^2-4*x^2*Dx^2-8*x*y*Dx*Dy-2*x^2*Dx
 -4*y^2*Dx*s+6*x*y*Dy+12*x*Dx*s-10*x*Dx-6*y*Dy+12*s

4 Annihilators of polynomial and rational functions

4.1 Annihilator of fαf^{\alpha} for α∈ℂ\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}

It is known (e. g. [34]) that for any α∈ℂ\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}, Dn/AnnDn⁡(fα)D_{n}/\ann_{D_{n}}(f^{\alpha}) is a holonomic DD-module. In the procedure annfspecial from dmod.lib we follow Algorithm 5.3.15 in [34]. Given ff and α\alpha, we compute AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)⊂Dn​[s]\Ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s})\subset D_{n}[s], the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of ff (cf. Section 6.1) and its minimal integer root s0s_{0}. Then, if α−(s0+1)∈ℕ\alpha-(s_{0}+1)\in{\mathbb{N}}, according to Algorithm 5.3.15 in [34] we have to compute a certain syzygy module in advance. Otherwise, AnnDn⁡(fα)=AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)∣s=α\ann_{D_{n}}(f^{\alpha})=\Ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s})\mid_{s=\alpha} is obtained via substitution.

Example 4.1.

In this example we show, how one computes the annihilator of 2​x​y2xy.

LIB "dmod.lib"; option(redSB); option(redTail);
ring r = 0,(x,y),dp; poly g = 2*x*y;
def A = Sannfs(g); setring A;        // compute Ann(g^s)
LD = groebner(LD); LD;               // GB of the ideal Ann(g^s)
==> LD[1]=y*Dy-s
==> LD[2]=x*Dx-s
def B = annfs0(LD,2*x*y); setring B; // compute BS polynomial
BS; // the list of roots and multiplicities of BS polynomial
==> [1]:
==>    _[1]=-1
==> [2]:
==>    2
// so, the minimal integer root is -1
setring A;                           // need to work with Ann(g^s) again
ideal I = annfspecial(LD,2*x*y,-1,1);
                       // the last argument 1 indicates that we want to compute f^1
print(matrix(I));                    // condensed presentation
==> Dy^2, y*Dy-1, Dx^2, x*Dx-1

4.2 Alternative for an annihilator of fmf^{m}

Computing a syzygy module in the previous algorithm can be expensive. Therefore we note, that for α=m∈ℕ\alpha=m\in{\mathbb{N}} we better use an easier approach.

Lemma 4.2.

Let g∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]g\in{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Consider the homomorphism of left DnD_{n}-modules ψ:Dn→Dn/⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩\psi:D_{n}\rightarrow D_{n}/\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle, ψ⁡(1)=g\psi(1)=g. Then AnnDn⁡(g)=ker⁡ψ\ann_{D_{n}}(g)=\ker\psi.

Proof.

Note, that 𝕂[x1,…,xn]≅Dn/⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\cong D_{n}/\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle as left DnD_{n}-modules. Hence we can view gg as the image of 11 under ψ\psi. Then AnnDn(g)={a∈Dn∣a∙g=0}={a∈Dn∣ag∈⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩}=kerψ\ann_{D_{n}}(g)=\{a\in D_{n}\mid a\bullet g=0\}=\{a\in D_{n}\mid ag\in\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle\}=\ker\psi. ∎

Remark 4.3.

Hence, given any element f∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], AnnDn⁡(f)\ann_{D_{n}}(f) can be computed via the kernel of a module homomorphism (algorithm Modulo) which amounts to just one Gröbner basis computation. Moreover, it does not use elimination and hence is clearly more efficient in the special case g=fng=f^{n} for f∈R,n∈ℕf\in R,n\in{\mathbb{N}}, than the more general method in Section 4.1. Notably this method can be generalized to various other operator algebras, see [35] for details. The corresponding procedure in dmodapp.lib is called annPoly.

Remark 4.4.

Yet another improvement can be achieved in the computation of the minimal integer root of the Bernstein-Sato polynomial with the algorithms from Theorem 6.6 below. Namely, since we know, that for an integer root, say α\alpha, of the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of a polynomial in n≥2n\geq 2 variables −n+1≤α≤−1-n+1\leq\alpha\leq-1 holds (by [33, 41]) and −1-1 is always a root, we can run the checkRoot procedure (which is just one Gröbner basis computation with an arbitrary ordering, see Section 6.4) starting from α=−n+1\alpha=-n+1 to α=−2\alpha=-2. We stop at the first affirmative answer from checkRoot or output −1-1 if no positive answer appears. Thus, one executes checkRoot at most n−2n-2 times.

Algorithm 4.5 (Heuristic for AnnDn⁡(fα)\Ann_{D_{n}}(f^{\alpha})).
0:  f∈ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]f\in{\mathbb{C}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}], α∈ℂ\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}
0:  AnnDn⁡(fα)\Ann_{D_{n}}(f^{\alpha})
 if α∈ℂ∖(ℤ∩[−n+1,−1])\alpha\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus({\mathbb{Z}}\cap[-n+1,-1]) then
   AnnDn⁡(fα)={⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩ if ​α=0,ker(Dn⟶1↦fmDn/⟨∂1,…,∂n⟩) if ​α=m∈ℕ,(cf. 4.2),AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)∣s=α if α∈(ℂ∖ℤ)∪(ℤ∩(−∞,−n]),\Ann_{D_{n}}(f^{\alpha})=\begin{cases}\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle&\text{ if }\alpha=0,\\ \ker(D_{n}\overset{1\mapsto f^{m}}{\longrightarrow}D_{n}/\langle\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n}\rangle)&\text{ if }\alpha=m\in{\mathbb{N}},\quad\text{(cf. \ \ref{annPoly})},\\ \Ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s})\mid_{s=\alpha}&\text{ if }\alpha\in({\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{Z}})\cup({\mathbb{Z}}\cap(-\infty,-n]),\end{cases}else (that is α∈ℤ∩[−n+1,−1]\alpha\in{\mathbb{Z}}\cap[-n+1,-1])
   μ:=min⁡{β∈ℤ<0∣bf​(β)=0}\mu:=\min\{\beta\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{<0}\mid b_{f}(\beta)=0\}
   AnnDn⁡(fα)={Procedure 4.1 with 4.4 if ​μ+1≤α≤−1,Procedure 4.4 and​AnnDn​[s]⁡(fs)∣s=α if −n+1≤α≤μ.\Ann_{D_{n}}(f^{\alpha})=\begin{cases}\text{Procedure \ref{annfA} with \ref{annPolyCheckRoot}}&\text{ if }\mu+1\leq\alpha\leq-1,\\ \text{Procedure \ref{annPolyCheckRoot} and}\Ann_{D_{n}[s]}(f^{s})\mid_{s=\alpha}&\text{ if }-n+1\leq\alpha\leq\mu.\\ \end{cases}
 end if

4.3 Annihilator of a rational function

In order to compute the annihilator II of a rational function fg\frac{f}{g} (it is known that Dn/ID_{n}/I is holonomic) we use the following lemma.

Lemma 4.6.

Let f,g∈𝕂⁡[x1,…,xn]∖{0}f,g\in{\mathbb{K}}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]\setminus\{0\}. Consider the homomorphism of left DnD_{n}-modules τ:Dn→Dn/AnnDn⁡(g−1),q↦q​f\tau:D_{n}\rightarrow D_{n}/\ann_{D_{n}}(g^{-1}),q\mapsto qf. Then AnnDn⁡(fg)=ker⁡τ\ann_{D_{n}}(\frac{f}{g})=\ker\tau.

Proof.

For q∈ker⁡τ={q∈Dn∣q​f∈AnnDn⁡(g−1)}q\in\ker\tau=\{q\in D_{n}\mid qf\in\ann_{D_{n}}(g^{-1})\}, (q​f)∙g−1=q∙(f​g−1)(qf)\bullet g^{-1}=q\bullet(fg^{-1}), hence AnnDn⁡(fg)=ker⁡τ\ann_{D_{n}}(\frac{f}{g})=\ker\tau. ∎

We compute AnnDn⁡(g−1)\ann_{D_{n}}(g^{-1}) with Algorithm 4.5 above. Although in the case, when −1-1 is not the minimal integer root of the Bernstein-Sato polynomial of gg, we have to use expensive algorithms like 4.1, we know no other methods to compute the annihilator in Weyl algebras. Also, no general algorithm for computing a complete system of operator equations (with operators including along partial differentiation also partial (qq-)differences et cetera) with polynomial coefficients, annihilating a rational function, is known to us. In our opinion, the existence of an algorithm for AnnDn⁡(g−1)\ann_{D_{n}}(g^{-1}) shows the intrinsic naturality of DD-modules compared with other linear operators acting on 𝕂⁡[x]{\mathbb{K}}[x]. The algorithm is implemented in dmodapp.lib and the corresponding procedure is called annRat.

Example 4.7.

In this example we demonstrate the computation of annihilators of a rational function. The procedure annRat takes as arguments polynomials in a commutative ring and returns a Weyl algebra (of type ring) together with an object of type ideal called LD (cf. Example 3.2). Note, that LD is given in a Gröbner basis.

LIB "dmodapp.lib";
ring r = 0,(x,y),dp;
poly g = 2*x*y;  poly f = x^2 - y^3; // we will compute Ann(g/f)
option(redSB); option(redTail);      // get reduced minimal GB
def B = annRat(g,f); setring B;
LD;                                  // Groebner basis of Ann(g/f)
==> LD[1]=3*x*Dx+2*y*Dy+1
==> LD[2]=y^3*Dy^2-x^2*Dy^2+6*y^2*Dy+6*y
==> LD[3]=9*y^2*Dx^2*Dy-4*y*Dy^3+27*y*Dx^2+2*Dy^2
==> LD[4]=y^4*Dy-x^2*y*Dy+2*y^3+x^2
==> LD[5]=9*y^3*Dx^2-4*y^2*Dy^2+10*y*Dy-10

5 bb-function with respect to weights for an ideal

Let 0≠w∈ℝ≥0n0\neq w\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}_{\geq 0} and consider the VV-filtration V={Vm∣m∈ℤ}V=\left\{V_{m}\mid m\in{\mathbb{Z}}\right\} on DnD_{n} with respect to ww, where VmV_{m} is spanned by {xα∂β∣−wα+wβ≤m}\left\{x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\mid-w\alpha+w\beta\leq m\right\} over 𝕂{\mathbb{K}}. That is, xix_{i} and ∂i\partial_{i} get weights −wi-w_{i} and wiw_{i} respectively. Note that then the relation ∂ixi=xi∂i+1\partial_{i}x_{i}=x_{i}\partial_{i}+1 is homogeneous of degree 00. It is known that the associated graded ring ⨁m∈ℤVm/Vm−1\bigoplus_{m\in{\mathbb{Z}}}V_{m}/V_{m-1} is isomorphic to DnD_{n}, which allows us to identify it with the Weyl algebra.

From now on we assume, that I⊂DnI\subset D_{n} is an ideal such that Dn/ID_{n}/I is a holonomic module. Since holonomic DD-modules are cyclic (e. g. [10]), for each holonomic DD-module MM there exists an ideal IMI_{M} such that M≅Dn/IMM\cong D_{n}/I_{M} as DD-modules.

Definition 5.1.

Let 0≠w∈ℝ≥0n0\neq w\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}_{\geq 0}. For a non-zero polynomial

p=∑α,β∈ℕ0ncα​βxα∂β∈Dnwith all but finitely many cα​β=0p=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}^{n}}c_{\alpha\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\in D_{n}\quad\text{with all but finitely many }c_{\alpha\beta}=0

we put m=maxα,β⁡{−w​α+w​β∣cα​β≠0}∈ℝm=\max_{\alpha,\beta}\{-w\alpha+w\beta\mid c_{\alpha\beta}\neq 0\}\in{\mathbb{R}} and define the initial form of pp with respect to the weight ww as follows:

in(−w,w)(p):=∑α,β∈ℕ0n:−w​α+w​β=mcα​βxα∂β.\ini_{(-w,w)}(p):=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}_{0}^{n}:~-w\alpha+w\beta=m}c_{\alpha\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}.

For the zero polynomial, we set in(−w,w)⁡(0):=0\ini_{(-w,w)}(0):=0. Additionally, the ideal in(−w,w)⁡(I):=𝕂⋅{in(−w,w)⁡(p)∣p∈I}\ini_{(-w,w)}(I):={\mathbb{K}}\cdot\{\ini_{(-w,w)}(p)\mid p\in I\} is called the initial ideal of II with respect to ww.

Definition 5.2.

Let 0≠w∈ℝ≥0n0\neq w\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}_{\geq 0} and s:=∑i=1nwixi∂is:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}x_{i}\partial_{i}. Then in(−w,w)⁡(I)∩𝕂⁡[s]\ini_{(-w,w)}(I)\cap{\mathbb{K}}[s] is a principal ideal in 𝕂⁡[s]{\mathbb{K}}[s]. Its monic generator bI,w​(s)b_{I,w}(s) is called the global bb-function of II with respect to the weight ww.

Theorem 5.3.

The global bb-function is nonzero.

We will give a proof of this well-known result in Section 5.2.

Following its definition, the computation of the global bb-function of II with respect to ww can be done in two steps:

  1. 1.

    Compute the initial ideal I′I^{\prime} of II with respect to ww.

  2. 2.

    Compute the intersection of I′I^{\prime} with the subalgebra 𝕂⁡[s]{\mathbb{K}}[s].

We will discuss both steps separately, starting with the initial ideal. It is important to mention, that although this procedure has been described in [34], this approach was completely treated by Noro in [30], accompanied with a very impressive implementation in Risa/Asir.

5.1 Computing the initial ideal

In order to compute the initial ideal, the method of weighted homogenization is proposed in [30], which we will describe below.

Let u,v∈ℝ>0nu,v\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}_{>0}. The GG-algebra D(u,v)(h):=𝕂⟨x1,…,xn,∂1,…,∂n,h∣{xjxi=xixj,∂j∂i=∂i∂j,xih=hxi,∂ih=h∂i,∂jxi=xi∂j+δi,jhui+vj}⟩D_{(u,v)}^{(h)}:={\mathbb{K}}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\partial_{1},\ldots,\partial_{n},h\mid\{x_{j}x_{i}=x_{i}x_{j},\partial_{j}\partial_{i}\\ =\partial_{i}\partial_{j},x_{i}h=hx_{i},\partial_{i}h=h\partial_{i},\partial_{j}x_{i}=x_{i}\partial_{j}+\delta_{i,j}h^{u_{i}+v_{j}}\}\rangle is called the nn-th weighted homogenized Weyl algebra with weights u,vu,v, i. e. xix_{i} and ∂i\partial_{i} get weights uiu_{i} and viv_{i} respectively.

For p=∑α,βcα​βxα∂β∈Dnp=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha\beta}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\in D_{n} we define the weighted homogenization of pp as follows:

H(u,v)(p)=∑α,βcα​βhdeg(u,v)⁡(p)−(u​α+v​β)xα∂β.H_{(u,v)}(p)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha\beta}h^{\deg_{(u,v)}(p)-(u\alpha+v\beta)}x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}.

This definition naturally extends to a set of polynomials. Here, deg(u,v)⁡(p)\deg_{(u,v)}(p) denotes the weighted total degree of pp with respect to weights u,vu,v for x,∂x,\partial and weight 11 for hh.

For a monomial ordering ≺\prec on DnD_{n}, which is not necessarily a well-ordering, we define an associated homogenized global ordering ≺(h)\prec^{(h)} in D(u,v)(h)D_{(u,v)}^{(h)} by setting h≺(h)xi,h≺(h)∂ih\prec^{(h)}x_{i},h\prec^{(h)}\partial_{i} for all ii and,

p≺(h)q\displaystyle p\prec^{(h)}q\quad if deg(u,v)⁡(p)\displaystyle\deg_{(u,v)}(p) <deg(u,v)⁡(q)\displaystyle<\deg_{(u,v)}(q)
or deg(u,v)⁡(p)\displaystyle\deg_{(u,v)}(p) =deg(u,v)(q)andp∣h=1≺q∣h=1.\displaystyle=\deg_{(u,v)}(q)\quad\text{and}\quad p_{\mid_{h=1}}\prec q_{\mid_{h=1}}.

Note that for u=v=(1,…,1)u=v=(1,\ldots,1) this is exactly the standard homogenization as in [34] and [9]. Analogue statements of the following two theorems can be found in [34] and [30] respectively.

Theorem 5.4.

Let FF be a finite subset of DnD_{n} and ≺\prec a global ordering. If G(h)G^{(h)} is a Gröbner basis of ⟨H(u,v)​(F)⟩\langle H_{(u,v)}(F)\rangle with respect to ≺(h)\prec^{(h)}, then G(h)∣h=1{G^{(h)}}_{\mid_{h=1}} is a Gröbner basis of ⟨F⟩\langle F\rangle with respect to ≺\prec.

Theorem 5.5.

Let ≺\prec be a global monomial ordering on DnD_{n} and ≺(−w,w)\prec_{(-w,w)} the non-global ordering defined by

xα∂β≺(−w,w)xγ∂δ\displaystyle x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\prec_{(-w,w)}x^{\gamma}\partial^{\delta}\quad if −w​α+w​β\displaystyle-w\alpha+w\beta <−w​γ+w​δ\displaystyle<-w\gamma+w\delta
or −w​α+w​β\displaystyle-w\alpha+w\beta =−wγ+wδandxα∂β≺xγ∂δ.\displaystyle=-w\gamma+w\delta\quad\text{and}\quad x^{\alpha}\partial^{\beta}\prec x^{\gamma}\partial^{\delta}.

If G(h)G^{(h)} is a Gröbner basis of H(u,v)​(I)H_{(u,v)}(I) with respect to ≺(h)(−w,w)\prec^{(h)}_{(-w,w)}, then the set {in(−w,w,0)⁡(g)∣g∈G(h)}\{\ini_{(-w,w,0)}(g)\mid g\in G^{(h)}\} is a Gröbner basis of in(−w,w,0)⁡(H(u,v)​(I))\ini_{(-w,w,0)}(H_{(u,v)}(I)) with respect to ≺(h)\prec^{(h)}.

Proof.

Let f′∈in(−w,w,0)⁡(H(u,v)​(I))f^{\prime}\in\ini_{(-w,w,0)}(H_{(u,v)}(I)) be (−w,w,0)(-w,w,0)-homogeneous. There exist f∈H(u,v)​(I)f\in H_{(u,v)}(I) and g∈G(h)g\in G^{(h)} such that f′=in(−w,w,0)⁡(f)f^{\prime}=\ini_{(-w,w,0)}(f) and lm≺(h)(−w,w)(g)∣lm≺(h)(−w,w)(f)\lm_{\prec^{(h)}_{(-w,w)}}(g)\mid\lm_{\prec^{(h)}_{(-w,w)}}(f). Summarizing the results from this section, we obtain the following algorithm to compute the initial ideal.

Algorithm 5.6 (InitialIdeal).
